claim: Heat stress leads to a decline in fertility in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: Consistent with previous studies, heat stress leads to a decline in fertility and micronuclei formation in pollen mother cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced silique length and pollen count at elevated temperatures (Figure 1).

claim: Heat stress leads to micronuclei formation in pollen mother cells.
source: Consistent with previous studies, heat stress leads to a decline in fertility and micronuclei formation in pollen mother cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased micronuclei at elevated temperatures (Figure 2B and C).

claim: Elevated temperature causes a decrease in the amount of centromeric histone at meiotic centromeres with increasing temperature.
source: Our results reveal that elevated temperature causes a decrease in the amount of centromeric histone and the kinetochore protein BMF1 at meiotic centromeres with increasing temperature.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence intensity measurements of eYFP:CENH3 on pachytene chromosomes at different temperatures (Figure 3A and B).

claim: Elevated temperature causes a decrease in the amount of kinetochore protein BMF1 at meiotic centromeres with increasing temperature.
source: Our results reveal that elevated temperature causes a decrease in the amount of centromeric histone and the kinetochore protein BMF1 at meiotic centromeres with increasing temperature.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence intensity measurements of BMF1:eYFP on pachytene chromosomes at different temperatures (Figure 3D and E).

claim: Heat stress increases the duration of meiotic divisions.
source: Furthermore, we show that heat stress increases the duration of meiotic divisions and prolongs the activity of the spindle assembly checkpoint during meiosis I, indicating an impaired efficiency of the kinetochore attachments to spindle microtubules.
evidence: Supported by live imaging data showing prolonged meiotic divisions at 30°C compared to 26°C (Figure 2A).

claim: Heat stress prolongs the activity of the spindle assembly checkpoint during meiosis I.
source: Furthermore, we show that heat stress increases the duration of meiotic divisions and prolongs the activity of the spindle assembly checkpoint during meiosis I, indicating an impaired efficiency of the kinetochore attachments to spindle microtubules.
evidence: Supported by measurements of BMF3:GFP signal duration at different temperatures (Figure 4B).

claim: Heat stress impairs the efficiency of kinetochore attachments to spindle microtubules.
source: Furthermore, we show that heat stress increases the duration of meiotic divisions and prolongs the activity of the spindle assembly checkpoint during meiosis I, indicating an impaired efficiency of the kinetochore attachments to spindle microtubules.
evidence: Inferred from prolonged SAC activity and increased meiotic division duration at elevated temperatures.

claim: Mutants with reduced levels of centromeric histone are sensitized to elevated temperature.
source: Our analysis of mutants with reduced levels of centromeric histone suggests that weakened centromeres sensitize plants to elevated temperature, resulting in meiotic defects and reduced fertility even at moderate temperatures.
evidence: Supported by data showing cenh3-4 mutants have reduced fertility at 26°C compared to wild type (Figure 1).

claim: Weakened centromeres result in meiotic defects at moderate temperatures in mutants with reduced centromeric histone.
source: Our analysis of mutants with reduced levels of centromeric histone suggests that weakened centromeres sensitize plants to elevated temperature, resulting in meiotic defects and reduced fertility even at moderate temperatures.
evidence: Supported by increased micronuclei formation in cenh3-4 at 26°C (Figure 2B and C).

claim: Weakened centromeres result in reduced fertility at moderate temperatures in mutants with reduced centromeric histone.
source: Our analysis of mutants with reduced levels of centromeric histone suggests that weakened centromeres sensitize plants to elevated temperature, resulting in meiotic defects and reduced fertility even at moderate temperatures.
evidence: Supported by pollen count and silique length data for cenh3-4 at 26°C (Figure 1).

claim: The structure and functionality of meiotic centromeres in Arabidopsis are highly sensitive to heat stress.
source: These results indicate that the structure and functionality of meiotic centromeres in Arabidopsis are highly sensitive to heat stress, and suggest that centromeres and kinetochores may represent a critical bottleneck in plant adaptation to increasing temperatures.
evidence: Inferred from the observed reduction in CENH3 and BMF1 at elevated temperatures and associated meiotic defects.

claim: Centromeres and kinetochores may represent a critical bottleneck in plant adaptation to increasing temperatures.
source: These results indicate that the structure and functionality of meiotic centromeres in Arabidopsis are highly sensitive to heat stress, and suggest that centromeres and kinetochores may represent a critical bottleneck in plant adaptation to increasing temperatures.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on the sensitivity of centromeres to heat stress and its impact on fertility.

claim: Global warming impacts crop productivity with more frequent and extreme heatwaves being particularly damaging.
source: Global warming impacts crop productivity with more frequent and extreme heatwaves being particularly damaging (Brás et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brás et al., 2021.

claim: Lower yields associated with heatwaves are mainly attributed to the impairment of the plant reproductive system.
source: The lower yields associated with heatwaves are mainly attributed to the impairment of the plant reproductive system (Lippmann et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lippmann et al., 2019.

claim: Male gametogenesis is particularly sensitive to higher temperatures.
source: Heat stress impairs both male and female reproductive structures, but male gametogenesis is particularly sensitive to higher temperatures (Zinn et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zinn et al., 2010.

claim: Heat stress affects pollen count, morphology, viability, dehiscence, germination, and pollen tube growth.
source: Studies in crop and non-crop species have shown that heat stress affects pollen count, morphology, viability, dehiscence, germination, and pollen tube growth (De Storme and Geelen, 2014; Chaturvedi et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Storme and Geelen, 2014 and Chaturvedi et al., 2021.

claim: Acute heat stress applied during microsporogenesis has the most detrimental effect on flower development.
source: Acute heat stress applied at different stages of flower development has been found to have the most detrimental effect during microsporogenesis (Pécrix et al., 2011; Hedhly et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pécrix et al., 2011 and Hedhly et al., 2020.

claim: Meiosis lasts approximately 1.5–2 days in Arabidopsis and barley.
source: It is a relatively slow process, lasting approximately 1.5–2 days in Arabidopsis and barley (Armstrong et al., 2003; Higgins et al., 2012; Prusicki et al., 2019; Valuchova et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Armstrong et al., 2003; Higgins et al., 2012; Prusicki et al., 2019; Valuchova et al., 2020.

claim: Elevated temperature alters the rate and distribution of meiotic recombination.
source: In prophase I, elevated temperature alters the rate and distribution of meiotic recombination (Higgins et al., 2012; Lloyd et al., 2018; Modliszewski et al., 2018) and a recent study in Arabidopsis has shown that heat shock response pathway directly regulates the recombination machinery (Kim et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Higgins et al., 2012; Lloyd et al., 2018; Modliszewski et al., 2018.

claim: Heat shock response pathway directly regulates the recombination machinery in Arabidopsis.
source: In prophase I, elevated temperature alters the rate and distribution of meiotic recombination (Higgins et al., 2012; Lloyd et al., 2018; Modliszewski et al., 2018) and a recent study in Arabidopsis has shown that heat shock response pathway directly regulates the recombination machinery (Kim et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2022.

claim: More severe heat stress can impair synapsis and pairing of homologous chromosomes.
source: More severe heat stress can impair synapsis and pairing of homologous chromosomes (Loidl, 1989; De Storme and Geelen, 2020; Ning et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Loidl, 1989; De Storme and Geelen, 2020; Ning et al., 2021.

claim: Impaired synapsis and pairing is likely due to inefficient completion of homologous recombination, which is monitored by specialized pachytene checkpoint.
source: This is likely due to inefficient completion of homologous recombination, which is monitored by specialized pachytene checkpoint (De Jaeger-Braet et al., 2022).
evidence: Inference supported by citation to De Jaeger-Braet et al., 2022.

claim: Elevated temperatures disturb spindle orientation during meiotic divisions and the formation of radial microtubule arrays, resulting in aberrant cytokinesis and diploid microspores.
source: Elevated temperatures disturb spindle orientation during meiotic divisions and the formation of radial microtubule arrays, resulting in aberrant cytokinesis and diploid microspores (Pécrix et al., 2011; De Storme and Geelen, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pécrix et al., 2011 and De Storme and Geelen, 2020.

claim: Acute heat stress leads to chromosome mis-segregation and the formation of micronuclei.
source: Furthermore, acute heat stress leads to chromosome mis-segregation and the formation of micronuclei (Wang et al., 2017; De Storme and Geelen, 2020; De Jaeger-Braet et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2017; De Storme and Geelen, 2020; De Jaeger-Braet et al., 2022.

claim: Meiotic micronuclei and chromosomal aberrations may arise as a consequence of abnormal repair of meiotic DNA breaks or homologous recombination intermediates in prophase I.
source: The meiotic micronuclei and chromosomal aberrations may arise as a consequence of abnormal repair of meiotic DNA breaks or homologous recombination intermediates in prophase I.
evidence: Speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: Meiotic micronuclei and chromosomal aberrations can be caused by defects in chromosome segregation during meiotic divisions.
source: However, they can also be caused by defects in chromosome segregation during meiotic divisions (Fenech et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fenech et al., 2011.

claim: Proper attachment of kinetochores to the spindle microtubules before anaphase is crucial for faithful chromosome partitioning to daughter cells.
source: Proper attachment of kinetochores to the spindle microtubules before anaphase is crucial for faithful chromosome partitioning to daughter cells, and this process is controlled by spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about kinetochore function.

claim: The process of kinetochore attachment to spindle microtubules is controlled by spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC).
source: Proper attachment of kinetochores to the spindle microtubules before anaphase is crucial for faithful chromosome partitioning to daughter cells, and this process is controlled by spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about SAC function.

claim: Micronuclei typically occur in mutants with impaired centromere/kinetochore structure or SAC when treated with spindle inhibitors.
source: Therefore, micronuclei typically occur in mutants with impaired centromere/kinetochore structure or SAC when treated with spindle inhibitors (Kalitsis et al., 2000; Lermontova et al., 2011a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kalitsis et al., 2000 and Lermontova et al., 2011a.

claim: In most eukaryotes centromeres are confined to a restricted region on each chromosome that serves as a platform for assembly of the kinetochore.
source: In most eukaryotes centromeres are confined to a restricted region on each chromosome that serves as a platform for assembly of the kinetochore, a multiprotein structure that connects chromosome with the spindle.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about centromere structure and function.

claim: The kinetochore is a multiprotein structure that connects chromosome with the spindle.
source: In most eukaryotes centromeres are confined to a restricted region on each chromosome that serves as a platform for assembly of the kinetochore, a multiprotein structure that connects chromosome with the spindle.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about kinetochore structure and function.

claim: Centromeres are defined epigenetically by a specialized centromeric histone H3 variant (CENH3).
source: Centromeres are defined epigenetically by a specialized centromeric histone H3 variant (CENH3), which forms the foundation for the recruitment of kinetochore proteins (McAinsh and Marston, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to McAinsh and Marston, 2022.

claim: CENH3 forms the foundation for the recruitment of kinetochore proteins.
source: Centromeres are defined epigenetically by a specialized centromeric histone H3 variant (CENH3), which forms the foundation for the recruitment of kinetochore proteins (McAinsh and Marston, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to McAinsh and Marston, 2022.

claim: In contrast to canonical histones, replicative dilution of CENH3 is not replenished immediately in S-phase, but in subsequent stages of the cell cycle.
source: In contrast to canonical histones, replicative dilution of CENH3 is not replenished immediately in S-phase, but in subsequent stages of the cell cycle (Stirpe and Heun, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stirpe and Heun, 2023.

claim: In plants, CENH3 is loaded on centromeres in G2 and persists there throughout the cell cycle.
source: In plants, CENH3 is loaded on centromeres in G2 and persists there throughout the cell cycle (Talbert et al., 2002; Lermontova et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Talbert et al., 2002 and Lermontova et al., 2006.

claim: CENH3 is a very stable component of centromeric chromatin.
source: CENH3 is a very stable component of centromeric chromatin, although its amount at centromeres gradually declines in terminally differentiated cells in plants and animals (Lermontova et al., 2011b; Swartz et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lermontova et al., 2011b and Swartz et al., 2019.

claim: The amount of CENH3 at centromeres gradually declines in terminally differentiated cells in plants and animals.
source: CENH3 is a very stable component of centromeric chromatin, although its amount at centromeres gradually declines in terminally differentiated cells in plants and animals (Lermontova et al., 2011b; Swartz et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lermontova et al., 2011b and Swartz et al., 2019.

claim: Heat stress significantly reduces the amount of CENH3 on meiotic chromosomes in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: In this study, we have discovered that heat stress significantly reduces the amount of CENH3 on meiotic chromosomes in Arabidopsis thaliana.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence intensity measurements (Figure 3).

claim: Loss of CENH3 leads to the formation of micronuclei.
source: This loss of CENH3 leads to the formation of micronuclei, which in turn contributes to the decrease in pollen formation and fertility in plants exposed to heat stress.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between reduced CENH3 and increased micronuclei at elevated temperatures.

claim: Formation of micronuclei contributes to the decrease in pollen formation and fertility in plants exposed to heat stress.
source: This loss of CENH3 leads to the formation of micronuclei, which in turn contributes to the decrease in pollen formation and fertility in plants exposed to heat stress.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between micronuclei formation and reduced fertility.

claim: Plants with a genetic mutation that reduces the amount of centromeric histone are more sensitive to moderately elevated temperature.
source: Additionally, we have found that plants with a genetic mutation that reduces the amount of centromeric histone are more sensitive to moderately elevated temperature.
evidence: Supported by data showing cenh3-4 mutants have reduced fertility at 26°C (Figure 1).

claim: Meiotic centromeres may represent a crucial point of vulnerability for plants in adaptation to raising temperatures.
source: These results suggest that meiotic centromeres may represent a crucial point of vulnerability for plants in adaptation to raising temperatures.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on the sensitivity of centromeres to heat stress.

claim: At 16°C, plants exhibited the slowest growth, but also the highest fertility, as assessed by pollen count and silique length.
source: At 16°C, plants exhibited the slowest growth, but also the highest fertility, as assessed by pollen count and silique length, which is indicative of seed yield (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1 showing highest pollen count and silique length at 16°C.

claim: Silique length is indicative of seed yield.
source: At 16°C, plants exhibited the slowest growth, but also the highest fertility, as assessed by pollen count and silique length, which is indicative of seed yield (Figure 1).
evidence: Established knowledge about the relationship between silique length and seed yield.

claim: Fertility slightly decreased at 21°C and further declined at 26°C.
source: Fertility slightly decreased at 21°C and further declined at 26°C.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1 showing progressive decline in pollen count and silique length.

claim: In cenh3-4 mutants, there is a sharp decline in pollen production and fertility at 26°C (86±48 pollen per anther).
source: In cenh3-4 mutants, we noticed a sharp decline in pollen production and fertility at 26°C (86±48 pollen per anther), whereas the fertility of the wild type was still relatively high (213±58 pollen per anther) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 1C.

claim: The fertility of wild type was still relatively high at 26°C (213±58 pollen per anther).
source: In cenh3-4 mutants, we noticed a sharp decline in pollen production and fertility at 26°C (86±48 pollen per anther), whereas the fertility of the wild type was still relatively high (213±58 pollen per anther) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 1C.

claim: Both cenh3-4 and wild type plants became infertile at 30°C.
source: Both cenh3-4 and wild type plants became infertile at 30°C.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1 showing minimal pollen production at 30°C.

claim: The heat-induced sterility was reversible and cenh3-4 as well as wild type plants transferred from 30°C to 21°C regained fertile flowers.
source: The heat-induced sterility was reversible and cenh3-4 as well as wild type plants transferred from 30°C to 21°C regained fertile flowers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C showing restored fertility.

claim: Pollen production and fertility gradually decline with increasing temperature.
source: These data indicate that pollen production and fertility gradually decline with increasing temperature and this trend is particularly pronounced in cenh3-4 mutants that have become almost sterile already at 26°C.
evidence: Inferred from the progressive decline observed across temperature conditions in Figure 1.

claim: The trend of declining fertility with increasing temperature is particularly pronounced in cenh3-4 mutants that have become almost sterile already at 26°C.
source: These data indicate that pollen production and fertility gradually decline with increasing temperature and this trend is particularly pronounced in cenh3-4 mutants that have become almost sterile already at 26°C.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1 showing sharp decline in cenh3-4 at 26°C.

claim: Extreme heat stress alters chromosome segregation fidelity and the duration of Arabidopsis meiosis.
source: It has been reported that extreme heat stress alters chromosome segregation fidelity and the duration of Arabidopsis meiosis (De Jaeger-Braet et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to De Jaeger-Braet et al., 2022.

claim: Temperatures of 34°C and above abolished chromosome pairing and synapsis and led to the formation of univalents.
source: Temperatures of 34°C and above abolished chromosome pairing and synapsis and led to the formation of univalents.
evidence: Statement about effects of extreme heat stress.

claim: Meiotic chromosomes are fully paired at 30°C.
source: However, meiotic chromosomes are fully paired at 30°C (Ning et al., 2021; De Jaeger-Braet et al., 2022; Fu et al., 2022), indicating that the recombination defects are not primarily responsible for abortive pollen development at this temperature.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ning et al., 2021; De Jaeger-Braet et al., 2022; Fu et al., 2022.

claim: Recombination defects are not primarily responsible for abortive pollen development at 30°C.
source: However, meiotic chromosomes are fully paired at 30°C (Ning et al., 2021; De Jaeger-Braet et al., 2022; Fu et al., 2022), indicating that the recombination defects are not primarily responsible for abortive pollen development at this temperature.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that chromosomes are fully paired at 30°C.

claim: Meiotic divisions were slowest at 16°C and lasted, on average, 441 and 459 min in wild type and cenh3-4, respectively.
source: Meiotic divisions were slowest at 16°C and lasted, on average, 441 and 459 min in wild type and cenh3-4, respectively (Videos 1 and 2, Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 2A and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Meiosis progressed significantly faster with increasing temperature.
source: Meiosis progressed significantly faster with increasing temperature.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2A showing reduced meiotic duration at higher temperatures.

claim: Wild type meiotic divisions took 169 min at 21°C and 142 min at 26°C.
source: Wild type meiotic divisions took 169 min at 21°C and 142 min at 26°C (Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2A and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: Meiotic divisions were also rapid in cenh3-4 at 21°C, lasting on average 156 min, but slowed down to 238 min at 26°C.
source: Meiotic divisions were also rapid in cenh3-4 at 21°C, lasting on average 156 min, but slowed down to 238 min at 26°C (Videos 5 and 6).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2A and Videos 5 and 6.

claim: In wild type, meiotic divisions occur at the fastest rate at 26°C.
source: This contrasts with the situation in wild type, where divisions occur at the fastest rate at 26°C.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2A showing shortest duration at 26°C for wild type.

claim: Meiotic divisions were prolonged at 30°C in both wild type and cenh3-4 mutants to 286 and 264 min, respectively.
source: Interestingly, meiotic divisions were prolonged at 30°C in both wild type and cenh3-4 mutants to 286 and 264 min, respectively (Videos 7 and 8).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2A and Videos 7 and 8.

claim: The slowdown of meiosis at 26°C and 30°C in cenh3-4, and at 30°C in wild type coincides with the steep decline of pollen production.
source: The slowdown of meiosis at 26°C and 30°C in cenh3-4, and at 30°C in wild type coincides with the steep decline of pollen production (Figure 1B and C) and indicates problems with meiotic progression.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between prolonged meiosis and reduced pollen production.

claim: The slowdown of meiosis at elevated temperatures indicates problems with meiotic progression.
source: The slowdown of meiosis at 26°C and 30°C in cenh3-4, and at 30°C in wild type coincides with the steep decline of pollen production (Figure 1B and C) and indicates problems with meiotic progression.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of prolonged meiosis at temperatures where fertility declines.

claim: Live imaging in cenh3-4 plants and, at 30°C, also in wild type showed formation of micronuclei that began to form during meiosis I and persisted till telophase II.
source: Live imaging in cenh3-4 plants and, at 30°C, also in wild type showed formation of micronuclei that began to form during meiosis I and persisted till telophase II (Videos 7 and 8).
evidence: Supported by observations in Videos 7 and 8.

claim: Micronuclei were apparent in cenh3-4 mutants at all temperatures.
source: The micronuclei were apparent in cenh3-4 mutants at all temperatures, which is consistent with partially impaired centromere function in these plants (Capitao et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2B and C and citation to Capitao et al., 2021.

claim: The occurrence of micronuclei in cenh3-4 is consistent with partially impaired centromere function in these plants.
source: The micronuclei were apparent in cenh3-4 mutants at all temperatures, which is consistent with partially impaired centromere function in these plants (Capitao et al., 2021).
evidence: Inference supported by citation to Capitao et al., 2021.

claim: The incidence of micronuclei in cenh3-4 substantially increased at 26°C.
source: Nevertheless, their occurrence substantially increased at 26°C and severe defects in chromosome segregation were observed at 30°C (Figure 2B and C; Videos 6 and 8) resulting in very few regular tetrads.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 2C.

claim: Severe defects in chromosome segregation were observed in cenh3-4 at 30°C resulting in very few regular tetrads.
source: Nevertheless, their occurrence substantially increased at 26°C and severe defects in chromosome segregation were observed at 30°C (Figure 2B and C; Videos 6 and 8) resulting in very few regular tetrads.
evidence: Supported by observations in Figure 2B and Videos 6 and 8.

claim: Micronuclei were occasionally detected at lower temperatures in wild type, albeit at a much lower level than in cenh3-4.
source: Whereas we occasionally detected micronuclei at lower temperatures also in wild type, albeit at a much lower level than in cenh3-4, their incidence increased 17-fold between 26°C and 30°C (Figure 2B and C, Videos 4 and 7).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: The incidence of micronuclei in wild type increased 17-fold between 26°C and 30°C.
source: Whereas we occasionally detected micronuclei at lower temperatures also in wild type, albeit at a much lower level than in cenh3-4, their incidence increased 17-fold between 26°C and 30°C (Figure 2B and C, Videos 4 and 7).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 2C.

claim: Dyads and polyads were observed at elevated temperatures.
source: In addition, we observed dyads and polyads, which is consistent with the previous study performed at a similar temperature (De Storme and Geelen, 2020).
evidence: Observation consistent with citation to De Storme and Geelen, 2020.

claim: Temperature-induced fertility reduction coincides with increased occurrence of micronuclei.
source: These data show that temperature-induced fertility reduction coincides with increased occurrence of micronuclei.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between fertility decline and micronuclei formation.

claim: Micronuclei may arise from acentric fragments and dicentric chromosomes derived from defective repair of meiotic breaks.
source: Micronuclei may arise from acentric fragments and dicentric chromosomes derived from defective repair of meiotic breaks.
evidence: Speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: Temperatures above 30°C were reported to cause aberrant recombination intermediates and induce pachytene checkpoint.
source: Indeed, temperatures above 30°C were reported to cause aberrant recombination intermediates and induce pachytene checkpoint (De Storme and Geelen, 2020; De Jaeger-Braet et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Storme and Geelen, 2020 and De Jaeger-Braet et al., 2022.

claim: Arabidopsis spo11-2 mutants do not form bivalents, and homologous chromosomes segregate randomly in anaphase I.
source: Arabidopsis spo11-2 mutants do not form bivalents, and homologous chromosomes segregate randomly in anaphase I (Stacey et al., 2006; Hartung et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stacey et al., 2006 and Hartung et al., 2007.

claim: Cytogenetic analysis in spo11-2 plants revealed a relatively high level of micronuclei in tetrads at 21°C.
source: Cytogenetic analysis in spo11-2 plants revealed a relatively high level of micronuclei in tetrads at 21°C (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Micronuclei in spo11-2 are likely generated by chromosome mis-segregation because unpaired univalents cannot properly biorient at metaphase I spindle.
source: Because unpaired univalents cannot properly biorient at metaphase I spindle, these micronuclei are likely generated by chromosome mis-segregation.
evidence: Inferred from the inability of univalents to properly biorient.

claim: Number of the micronuclei almost doubled in spo11-2 plants grown at 30°C.
source: Importantly, number of the micronuclei almost doubled in spo11-2 plants grown at 30°C (Figure 2B and C) arguing that temperature has a direct effect on chromosome segregation.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 2C.

claim: Temperature has a direct effect on chromosome segregation.
source: Importantly, number of the micronuclei almost doubled in spo11-2 plants grown at 30°C (Figure 2B and C) arguing that temperature has a direct effect on chromosome segregation.
evidence: Inferred from increased micronuclei in spo11-2 at elevated temperature.

claim: A. thaliana usually flowers from March to early summer under average daily temperatures lower than the ones used for cultivation in laboratories.
source: In its natural habitats, A. thaliana usually flowers from March to early summer under average daily temperatures lower than the ones used for cultivation in laboratories (Shindo et al., 2007; Brachi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shindo et al., 2007 and Brachi et al., 2010.

claim: In natural habitats, A. thaliana never experiences sustained temperatures over 30°C due to the day-night cycle.
source: Due to the day-night cycle, they never experience sustained temperatures over 30°C.
evidence: Inference based on natural temperature fluctuations.

claim: A drastic reduction in fertility and pollen count was observed under the 18°C/34°C night/day regime compared to control plants grown under the 18°C/21°C night/day regime.
source: We observed a drastic reduction in fertility and pollen count, as well as an increased frequency of micronuclei compared to control plants grown under the 18°C/21°C night/day regime (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–D.

claim: An increased frequency of micronuclei was observed under the 18°C/34°C night/day regime compared to control plants grown under the 18°C/21°C night/day regime.
source: We observed a drastic reduction in fertility and pollen count, as well as an increased frequency of micronuclei compared to control plants grown under the 18°C/21°C night/day regime (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Heatwaves occurring during flowering can have a detrimental effect on Arabidopsis meiosis.
source: These data suggest that heatwaves occurring during flowering can have a detrimental effect on Arabidopsis meiosis.
evidence: Inferred from the effects observed under the 18°C/34°C day/night regime.

claim: cenh3-4 mutants grown at 26°C exhibit the same behavior as wild type plants grown at 30°C.
source: Our phenotypic analysis indicates that cenh3-4 mutants grown at 26°C exhibit the same behavior as wild type plants grown at 30°C.
evidence: Inferred from similar levels of fertility reduction and micronuclei formation.

claim: CENH3 is present on meiotic chromosomes from early prophase I.
source: CENH3 is present on meiotic chromosomes from early prophase I (Talbert et al., 2002; Lermontova et al., 2006) and its signal is most visible in pachytene when homologous chromosomes are fully synapsed.
evidence: Supported by citations to Talbert et al., 2002 and Lermontova et al., 2006.

claim: The CENH3 signal is most visible in pachytene when homologous chromosomes are fully synapsed.
source: CENH3 is present on meiotic chromosomes from early prophase I (Talbert et al., 2002; Lermontova et al., 2006) and its signal is most visible in pachytene when homologous chromosomes are fully synapsed.
evidence: Observation about CENH3 signal visibility during meiosis.

claim: eYFP:CENH3 was readily detectable on pachytene chromosomes at 21°C, but the signal decreased significantly at 26°C and declined further at 30°C.
source: While eYFP:CENH3 was readily detectable on pachytene chromosomes at 21°C, the signal decreased significantly at 26°C and declined further at 30°C (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 3B.

claim: The eYFP:CENH3 signal in tapetum nuclei adjacent to pollen mother cells exhibited the opposite trend and increased with elevated temperature.
source: In contrast, the eYFP:CENH3 signal in tapetum nuclei adjacent to pollen mother cells (PMCs) exhibited the opposite trend and increased with elevated temperature (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 3C.

claim: At 30°C, the tapetum exhibited a strong eYFP:CENH3 signal, whereas the signal on pachytene chromosomes in the same field of view was barely detectable.
source: This resulted in a striking difference in signal intensity at 30°C, where the tapetum exhibited a strong eYFP:CENH3 signal, whereas the signal on pachytene chromosomes in the same field of view was barely detectable (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by images in Figure 3A.

claim: Elevated temperature reduces the level of CENH3 on pachytene chromosomes in non-tagged wild type plants as validated by immunodetection using a CENH3 antibody.
source: We validated the observation that elevated temperature reduces the level of CENH3 on pachytene chromosomes also in non-tagged wild type plants by immunodetection using a CENH3 antibody (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunodetection data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: BMF1 is an Arabidopsis BUB1-related protein that associates with centromeres throughout the cell cycle.
source: BMF1 is an Arabidopsis BUB1-related protein that associates with centromeres throughout the cell cycle (Komaki and Schnittger, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Komaki and Schnittger, 2017.

claim: BMF1 co-localizes with CENH3 from early prophase I to telophase II.
source: We generated Arabidopsis marker lines expressing BMF1::BMF1:eYFP and BMF1::BMF1:TagRFP constructs, and validated BMF1 co-localization with CENH3 from early prophase I to telophase II (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Video 9).
evidence: Supported by observations in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Video 9.

claim: BMF1 signal was not detected in roots or in meiotic cells of cenh3-4 mutants.
source: The BMF1 signal was not detected in roots or in meiotic cells of cenh3-4 mutants indicating that BMF1 loading on centromeres is CENH3 dependent (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by observations in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: BMF1 loading on centromeres is CENH3 dependent.
source: The BMF1 signal was not detected in roots or in meiotic cells of cenh3-4 mutants indicating that BMF1 loading on centromeres is CENH3 dependent (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Inferred from absence of BMF1 signal in cenh3-4 mutants.

claim: Analysis of the BMF1:eYFP signal in wild type plants grown at elevated temperatures showed a decrease in the signal on pachytene chromosomes at 26°C, and BMF1 was undetectable at 30°C.
source: Analysis of the BMF1:eYFP signal in wild type plants grown at elevated temperatures showed a decrease in the signal on pachytene chromosomes at 26°C, and BMF1 was undetectable at 30°C (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 3E.

claim: Similar to CENH3, elevated temperature reduces the kinetochore protein BMF1 at meiotic centromeres.
source: These data suggest that similar to CENH3, elevated temperature reduces the kinetochore protein BMF1 at meiotic centromeres.
evidence: Inferred from the observed reduction in BMF1 signal at elevated temperatures.

claim: Reduced amount of CENH3 and smaller centromeres prolong the biorientation of mitotic chromosomes in cenh3-4 plants.
source: In our previous report, we showed that reduced amount of CENH3 and smaller centromeres prolong the biorientation of mitotic chromosomes in cenh3-4 plants (Capitao et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Capitao et al., 2021.

claim: Biorientation is monitored by the SAC and its satisfaction triggers anaphase.
source: Biorientation is monitored by the SAC and its satisfaction triggers anaphase.
evidence: Established knowledge about SAC function.

claim: Meiotic chromosomes with heat-induced reductions in CENH3 might take longer to properly attach to the spindle and satisfy the SAC.
source: We hypothesized that meiotic chromosomes with heat-induced reductions in CENH3 might take longer to properly attach to the spindle and satisfy the SAC.
evidence: Hypothesis based on previous observations in mitotic cells.

claim: The core SAC proteins temporarily associate with the kinetochore during spindle formation and disappear just before the onset of anaphase.
source: The core SAC proteins temporarily associate with the kinetochore during spindle formation and disappear just before the onset of anaphase.
evidence: Established knowledge about SAC protein dynamics.

claim: BMF3 is one of the core components of the Arabidopsis SAC, which associates with the kinetochores during prometaphase and extends this association in the presence of a spindle inhibitor.
source: BMF3 is one of the core components of the Arabidopsis SAC, which associates with the kinetochores during prometaphase and extends this association in the presence of a spindle inhibitor (Komaki and Schnittger, 2017; Lampou et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Komaki and Schnittger, 2017 and Lampou et al., 2023.

claim: BMF3 has previously only been analyzed in the context of mitosis.
source: First, we validated the localization of BMF3 on meiotic chromosomes by live cell imaging, as BMF3 has previously only been analyzed in the context of mitosis (Komaki and Schnittger, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Komaki and Schnittger, 2017.

claim: The BMF3:GFP signal was observed during prometaphase/metaphase I, disappeared at the onset of anaphase I and reappeared again during metaphase II.
source: We observed the BMF3:GFP signal during prometaphase/metaphase I, it disappeared at the onset of anaphase I and reappeared again during metaphase II, suggesting that BMF3 is a component of the meiotic SAC (Figure 4A, Video 10).
evidence: Supported by observations in Figure 4A and Video 10.

claim: BMF3 is a component of the meiotic SAC.
source: We observed the BMF3:GFP signal during prometaphase/metaphase I, it disappeared at the onset of anaphase I and reappeared again during metaphase II, suggesting that BMF3 is a component of the meiotic SAC (Figure 4A, Video 10).
evidence: Inferred from the temporal pattern of BMF3:GFP signal during meiosis.

claim: The BMF3:GFP signal persisted for an average approximately 22.7 min at 21°C and 26°C, but its appearance was prolonged to 40.5 min at 30°C.
source: We observed that while the BMF3:GFP signal persisted for an average approximately 22.7 min at 21°C and 26°C, its appearance was prolonged to 40.5 min at 30°C (Figure 4B, Videos 11 and 12).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 4B.

claim: The intensity of the BMF3 signal appeared to decrease with increasing temperature.
source: We also noticed that the intensity of the BMF3 signal appeared to decrease with increasing temperature (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by observations in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A weaker but prolonged association of BMF3 with the meiosis I kinetochore was also observed in cenh3-4 mutants with reduced levels of centromeric histone.
source: A weaker but prolonged association of BMF3 with the meiosis I kinetochore was also observed in cenh3-4 mutants with reduced levels of centromeric histone (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Elevated temperature leads to partial depletion of CENH3 and impairment of centromere structure, which may prolong the time required for chromosome biorientation and SAC satisfaction.
source: These observations are consistent with the notion that elevated temperature leads to partial depletion of CENH3 and impairment of centromere structure, which may prolong the time required for chromosome biorientation and SAC satisfaction.
evidence: Inference based on the observed prolonged SAC activity and reduced CENH3 at elevated temperatures.

claim: A. thaliana (ecotype Col-0) exhibited the highest fertility when grown at 16°C, which closely resembles the average temperature during flowering in its natural habitats.
source: We observed that A. thaliana (ecotype Col-0) exhibited the highest fertility when grown at 16°C, which closely resembles the average temperature during flowering in its natural habitats (Brachi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1 and citation to Brachi et al., 2010.

claim: At 16°C, meiotic divisions took more than twice as long as at 21°C.
source: At this temperature, meiotic divisions took more than twice as long as at 21°C.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: Arabidopsis grown at 17°C was reported to exhibit slower microsporogenesis, with the entire meiosis process lasting 48 hr as opposed to 32 hr at 24°C.
source: Arabidopsis grown at 17°C was reported to exhibit slower microsporogenesis, with the entire meiosis process lasting 48 hr as opposed to 32 hr at 24°C (Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2020.

claim: The slower progression at lower temperature was found to be less detrimental for several mutations that affect microsporogenesis, indicating that a slower pace provides greater robustness.
source: Interestingly, the slower progression was found to be less detrimental for several mutations that affect microsporogenesis, indicating that a slower pace provides greater robustness.
evidence: Inference based on observations about mutation effects at different temperatures.

claim: The pace of meiosis in Arabidopsis is well optimized for its natural growth conditions, enabling the plants to achieve maximum fitness.
source: Overall, these observations suggest that the pace of meiosis in Arabidopsis is well optimized for its natural growth conditions, enabling the plants to achieve maximum fitness.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on observations about fertility at different temperatures.

claim: The process of meiosis is progressively accelerated with increasing temperature.
source: The process of meiosis is progressively accelerated with increasing temperature (De Jaeger-Braet et al., 2022; Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2 and citation to De Jaeger-Braet et al., 2022.

claim: The speed of meiotic divisions reaches its maximum at 26°C and slows down at 30°C under the conditions used in this study.
source: However, the speed of meiotic divisions reaches its maximum at 26°C and slows down at 30°C under the conditions used in this study.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: At 30°C, fertility is lost and high incidence of micronuclei is observed, implying that the temperature around 30°C impairs some molecular processes involved in chromosome segregation and genome integrity.
source: At 30°C, fertility is lost and high incidence of micronuclei is observed, implying that the temperature around 30°C impairs some molecular processes involved in chromosome segregation and genome integrity.
evidence: Inferred from the observed loss of fertility and increased micronuclei at 30°C.

claim: The impact of temperature on recombination machinery is well documented.
source: The impact of temperature on recombination machinery is well documented.
evidence: General statement about established knowledge.

claim: A moderate increase in temperature leads to shift in chiasma distribution and cross-over frequency.
source: A moderate increase in temperature leads to shift in chiasma distribution and cross-over frequency (Higgins et al., 2012; Lloyd et al., 2018; Modliszewski et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Higgins et al., 2012; Lloyd et al., 2018; Modliszewski et al., 2018.

claim: Heat stress above 30°C severely impairs recombination and synapsis, leading to univalents and chromosome segregation defects.
source: Heat stress above 30°C severely impairs recombination and synapsis, leading to univalents and chromosome segregation defects (De Storme and Geelen, 2020; Ning et al., 2021; De Jaeger-Braet et al., 2022; Fu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Storme and Geelen, 2020; Ning et al., 2021; De Jaeger-Braet et al., 2022; Fu et al., 2022.

claim: Only a portion of micronuclei is derived from aberrant recombination.
source: Nevertheless, we observed an increased incidence of micronuclei also in SPO11-deficient plants that do not form meiotic DNA double-strand breaks indicating that only a portion of micronuclei is derived from aberrant recombination.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of micronuclei in spo11 mutants.

claim: Recent reports have indicated that the stability of microtubules in plant meiocytes is compromised by heat stress.
source: Recent reports have indicated that the stability of microtubules in plant meiocytes is compromised by heat stress (Wang et al., 2017; De Jaeger-Braet et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2017 and De Jaeger-Braet et al., 2022.

claim: High temperature affects the structure and function of meiotic centromeres.
source: In this study, we have demonstrated that high temperature also affects the structure and function of meiotic centromeres.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced CENH3 and BMF1 at elevated temperatures.

claim: Weakened centromeres may be less effective in establishing productive interactions with spindle microtubules.
source: These weakened centromeres may be less effective in establishing productive interactions with spindle microtubules.
evidence: Speculative statement about the consequences of reduced centromere proteins.

claim: The prolonged SAC observed through the longer residency of BMF3 on prometaphase I centromeres at 30°C is consistent with weakened centromeres being less effective in establishing productive interactions with spindle microtubules.
source: This is consistent with the prolonged SAC we observed through the longer residency of BMF3 on prometaphase I centromeres at 30°C (Figure 4).
evidence: Inference based on the observed prolonged SAC activity.

claim: Heat stress impairs centromere function, which in turn decreases the efficiency of proper attachment of chromosomes to the meiotic spindle.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that heat stress impairs centromere function, which in turn decreases the efficiency of proper attachment of chromosomes to the meiotic spindle.
evidence: Inference based on multiple lines of evidence including reduced CENH3, prolonged SAC, and increased micronuclei.

claim: Chromosomes with impaired centromere function may not be transported to their intended destination in a timely manner and, therefore, not incorporated into the newly formed nuclei.
source: As a result, these chromosomes may not be transported to their intended destination in a timely manner and, therefore, not incorporated into the newly formed nuclei.
evidence: Speculative explanation for micronuclei formation.

claim: The increased temperature sensitivity of cenh3-4 plants is explained by the fact that they already have smaller centromeres.
source: This scenario also explains the increased temperature sensitivity of cenh3-4 plants, which already have smaller centromeres (Capitao et al., 2021); even moderately elevated temperature may further enhance this defect.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that cenh3-4 has reduced centromere size and is more sensitive to heat.

claim: Studies in human cells have revealed that CENH3 nucleosomes are less stable than previously thought.
source: Studies in human cells have revealed that CENH3 nucleosomes are less stable than previously thought.
evidence: General statement about findings in human cells.

claim: The amount of CENH3 at centromeres declines over time and must be actively replenished to preserve centromere identity and proliferative potential.
source: The amount of CENH3 at centromeres declines over time and must be actively replenished to preserve centromere identity and proliferative potential (Swartz et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Swartz et al., 2019.

claim: Transcription has been shown to cause the eviction of pre-existing CENH3 from the centromeres.
source: Transcription has been shown to cause the eviction of pre-existing CENH3 from the centromeres (Swartz et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Swartz et al., 2019.

claim: Depletion of CENH3 from centromeres has been observed in leaf cells with increasing age in Arabidopsis, indicating that this phenomenon also occurs in plants.
source: In Arabidopsis, depletion of CENH3 from centromeres has been observed in leaf cells with increasing age, indicating that this phenomenon also occurs in plants (Lermontova et al., 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lermontova et al., 2011b.

claim: The Arabidopsis centromeric satellite repeat CEN180 undergoes pervasive transcription, which is largely repressed by epigenetic silencing mechanisms.
source: The Arabidopsis centromeric satellite repeat CEN180 undergoes pervasive transcription, which is largely repressed by epigenetic silencing mechanisms (May et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to May et al., 2005.

claim: Heat stress can alleviate the repression and induce transcription of CEN180 from silent loci.
source: However, heat stress can alleviate the repression and induce transcription of CEN180 from silent loci (Tittel-Elmer et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tittel-Elmer et al., 2010.

claim: Temperature-induced transcription can increase the eviction of CENH3 nucleosomes, potentially compromising centromere structure if not replenished.
source: This temperature-induced transcription can increase the eviction of CENH3 nucleosomes, potentially compromising centromere structure if not replenished.
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on known effects of transcription on CENH3 eviction.

claim: Tapetum cells do not exhibit CENH3 loss at elevated temperatures in contrast to PMCs.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to PMCs, tapetum cells do not exhibit CENH3 loss at elevated temperatures (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: The difference in CENH3 levels between PMCs and tapetum cells at elevated temperatures may be due to the different efficiency of CENH3 deposition to replenish the heat-induced loss of CENH3 in these cell types.
source: This may be due to the different efficiency of CENH3 deposition to replenish the heat-induced loss of CENH3 in these cell types.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed difference.

claim: Arabidopsis meiotic cells possess a specialized CENH3 loading mechanism that seems more stringent than the loading mechanism operating in mitotic cells.
source: Accordingly, Arabidopsis meiotic cells possess a specialized CENH3 loading mechanism that seems more stringent than the loading mechanism operating in mitotic cells (Lermontova et al., 2011a; Ravi et al., 2011; Schubert et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lermontova et al., 2011a; Ravi et al., 2011; Schubert et al., 2014.

claim: Crosses between wild type and plants with altered CENH3 can result in postzygotic loss of one set of parental chromosomes.
source: Crosses between wild type and plants with altered CENH3 can result in postzygotic loss of one set of parental chromosomes (Ravi and Chan, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ravi and Chan, 2010.

claim: Postzygotic chromosome loss is attributed to inefficient re-loading of CENH3 on the set of parental chromosomes with the altered centromeres in hybrid embryos.
source: This is attributed to inefficient re-loading of CENH3 on the set of parental chromosomes with the altered centromeres in hybrid embryos (Marimuthu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marimuthu et al., 2021.

claim: Heat stress applied during early embryogenesis could enhance the centromere-mediated genome elimination in Arabidopsis.
source: Recent studies showed that heat stress applied during early embryogenesis could enhance the centromere-mediated genome elimination in Arabidopsis (Ahmadli et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ahmadli et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023.

claim: Elevated temperature can destabilize centromeres in embryonic cells similarly to meiocytes.
source: This indicates that similarly to meiocytes, elevated temperature can also destabilize centromeres in embryonic cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that heat stress enhances genome elimination in embryos.

claim: Already moderate increase in temperature has a discernable effect on pollen production and silique length.
source: We found that already moderate increase in temperature has a discernable effect on pollen production and silique length, and exposure to 30°C impairs the structure of centromeres and leads to plant sterility.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Exposure to 30°C impairs the structure of centromeres and leads to plant sterility.
source: We found that already moderate increase in temperature has a discernable effect on pollen production and silique length, and exposure to 30°C impairs the structure of centromeres and leads to plant sterility.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced CENH3 and fertility loss at 30°C.

claim: Rising temperatures and more frequent weather extreme periods pose a threat to global food security by disrupting plant reproductive processes.
source: These findings are particularly relevant in the context of climate change, where rising temperatures and more frequent weather extreme periods pose a threat to global food security by disrupting plant reproductive processes.
evidence: General statement about climate change impacts.

claim: The study provides important insights into the mechanisms that contribute to the reduction of plant fertility in response to elevated temperature.
source: As such, our study provides important insights into the mechanisms that contribute to the reduction of plant fertility in response to elevated temperature.
evidence: Summary statement about the study's contribution.

claim: Further research on molecular aspects underlying heat stress effects may help to develop strategies to generate plants more resilient to extreme weather during their reproductive phase.
source: Further research on molecular aspects underlying these effects may help to develop strategies to generate plants more resilient to extreme weather during their reproductive phase.
evidence: Speculative statement about future applications.

claim: The cenh3-4 allele of Arabidopsis centromeric histone CENH3 carries a mutation in the splicing donor site of the third exon.
source: In our previous work, we identified the cenh3-4 allele of Arabidopsis centromeric histone CENH3 that carries a mutation in the splicing donor site of the third exon (Capitao et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Capitao et al., 2021.

claim: The cenh3-4 mutation leads to a 10-fold reduction in fully spliced CENH3 mRNA and a decreased amount of centromeric histone.
source: This leads to a 10-fold reduction in fully spliced CENH3 mRNA and a decreased amount of centromeric histone.
evidence: Statement about the molecular consequences of the cenh3-4 mutation.

claim: cenh3-4 plants have smaller centromeres and are sensitive to oryzalin.
source: Consequently, cenh3-4 plants have smaller centromeres and are sensitive to oryzalin (Capitao et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Capitao et al., 2021.

claim: Under standard conditions, cenh3-4 mutants are barely distinguishable from wild type.
source: Under standard conditions, cenh3-4 mutants are barely distinguishable from wild type, but we noticed their reduced fertility when grown at an elevated temperature.
evidence: Observation about cenh3-4 phenotype under standard conditions.
